raw_response:
Well, let me think through this year's plan. I'm 69 now, been on this land for 15 years, and my body doesn't move the way it used to. My wife helps me, but two of the kids work off-farm in town, so most of the heavy work falls on the two of us and some hired hands when we really need them. Eighteen mu isn't a lot, but for an old couple it's plenty of work.

**Wheat-maize, about 10 mu.** This is my backbone. I've done this rotation for years and I know what it needs. I'll put the wheat in around early-to-mid October after the maize comes off. I usually buy certified seed from the co-op — the saved seed gets weaker after a few years, the extension fellow told me that and I've seen it myself. For fertilizer on wheat, I put down a compound NPK (15-15-15) as base fertilizer before sowing, about two bags per mu, then topdress with urea at the jointing stage in spring. All told that comes out around 16-17 kg N/mu. I irrigate the wheat at winter, jointing, and heading — three times usually, sometimes a fourth if it's a dry spring. The well is metered so I don't waste.

Then the maize goes in right after wheat harvest in mid-June. Tight turnaround, maybe three to five days. No time to plow proper — I use no-till direct seeding with a rented planter. Base fertilizer mixed with seed, then topdress once at the big trumpet stage. Maize needs less water than wheat here, usually one or two irrigations if July-August rains are decent.

**Cotton, about 5 mu** on the western piece where the soil is a bit saltier — cotton handles that better than grain. I plant end of April. Cotton is more trouble than it used to be — picking is hard on my back and hired hands cost more every year. But the price has been okay and I've grown it for years so I know it. Moderate fertilizer, and I spray for bollworm when I see them.

**Chili, 3 mu.** This is our cash crop, the one that actually brings real money if the price holds. I start seedlings in a small plot and transplant in late April. Chili eats fertilizer and drinks water, but the return per mu is several times grain. My daughter-in-law helps with picking in September. It's risky — if the price drops, we're just working for nothing — but last year was decent so I'll keep the same 3 mu.

I'm keeping most things the same as last year. At my age I don't experiment much. If something worked, I do it again.
